capsules.subject: NCERT Quick Notes
capsules.title: NCERT Quick Notes — Human Physiology I: Digestion & Breathing
capsules.body:
Digestion (NCERT lines that get asked)
Teeth formula (adult): 2123/2123 · Dental heterodont + diphyodont · Common duct of liver + pancreas = hepatopancreatic duct, guarded by sphincter of Oddi
Salivary amylase works at pH ≈ 6.8; pepsin at pH 1.8–2 (inactive pepsinogen activated by HCl) · Rennin only in infants
Bile has NO enzymes — it emulsifies fat · Trypsinogen → trypsin by enteropeptidase (enterokinase) of duodenal juice
Absorption: glucose/amino acids → blood capillaries; fatty acids + glycerol → lacteals (lymph) · Villi + microvilli multiply surface area · Succus entericus = intestinal juice

Breathing
Volumes: TV 500 mL · IRV 2500–3000 · ERV 1000–1100 · RV 1100–1200 mL · Vital capacity ≈ 4600 mL (ERV + TV + IRV)
IC = TV + IRV · FRC = ERV + RV · Total lung capacity ≈ 5100–5800 mL
97% O₂ carried by RBC (haemoglobin), 3% dissolved · CO₂: 70% as bicarbonate, 20–25% carbamino-haemoglobin, 7% dissolved
Respiratory centre: medulla (rhythm) + pons (pneumotaxic — can moderate) · Every 100 mL oxygenated blood delivers ≈ 5 mL O₂ to tissues at rest

capsules.subject: NCERT Quick Notes
capsules.title: NCERT Quick Notes — Human Physiology II: Circulation & Excretion
capsules.body:
Body fluids & circulation
Cardiac cycle = 0.8 s at 72 bpm · Stroke volume ≈ 70 mL ⇒ cardiac output ≈ 5000 mL/min
Joint diastole = 0.4 s · First heart sound “lubb” = AV valves closing; “dubb” = semilunar valves
SA node = pacemaker (max autorhythmicity) · Bundle of His → Purkinje fibres spread the impulse over ventricles
Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg · Portal system: hepatic portal vein carries blood from gut to liver before the heart
Lymph: returns interstitial fluid to blood; fats absorbed via lacteals enter lymph first

Excretion
Nephron: glomerulus + Bowman’s capsule → PCT → Henle’s loop → DCT → collecting duct
GFR ≈ 180 litres/day; ≈ 99% reabsorbed · PCT reabsorbs ~70–80% of filtrate + all glucose
Descending limb of Henle: permeable to water, not salts; ascending limb: opposite
Counter-current: Henle’s loop + vasa recta · ADH (vasopressin) acts on DCT/collecting duct; aldosterone on Na⁺ uptake
Urea cycle (ornithine cycle) runs in the liver · Dialysis fluid has no nitrogenous wastes — that gradient drives diffusion

capsules.subject: NCERT Quick Notes
capsules.title: NCERT Quick Notes — Human Physiology III: Neural & Chemical Coordination
capsules.body:
Neural control
Resting potential ≈ −70 mV (Na⁺/K⁺ pump: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) · Threshold stimulus opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → depolarisation
Synapse: electrical (fast, rare) vs chemical (neurotransmitter, synaptic cleft) · Myelin speeds conduction; nodes of Ranvier = saltatory conduction
Medulla: respiratory, cardiovascular and gastric reflexes · Hypothalamus: temperature, hunger, thirst — “smart control room”
Midbrain corpora quadrigemina (visual/auditory reflexes) · Cerebellum: posture + balance (alcohol affects it first)

Endocrine snap-facts
Hypothalamus → releasing/inhibiting hormones; somatostatin inhibits GH · Gigantism/acromegaly = GH excess; cretinism = hypothyroid in childhood, myxedema in adults
Insulin: β-cells; glucagon: α-cells of islets of Langerhans · Diabetes mellitus — insulin deficiency; diabetes insipidus — ADH deficiency
Adrenal medulla = emergency hormones (epinephrine/norepinephrine, “3F”); cortex — cortisol (glucocorticoid), aldosterone (mineralocorticoid)
Thymus shrinks with age (thymosin, T-lymphocyte maturation) · PTH raises blood Ca²⁺; calcitonin (thyroid) lowers it — antagonistic pair

capsules.subject: NCERT Quick Notes
capsules.title: NCERT Quick Notes — Genetics I: Principles of Inheritance
capsules.body:
Ratios to recall instantly
Monohybrid F₂: phenotype 3:1, genotype 1:2:1 · Dihybrid F₂: 9:3:3:1 · Test cross: 1:1 (monohybrid), 1:1:1:1 (dihybrid)
Incomplete dominance (snapdragon): F₂ = 1:2:1 both ways · Codominance: AB blood group (IAIB)
Multiple alleles: ABO group — IA, IB, i on chromosome 9 (gene I)

Linkage & sex determination
Morgan — Drosophila; linkage strength inversely proportional to distance; 1 map unit = 1% recombination (max 50%)
XX–XY: humans, Drosophila · XX–XO: grasshopper · ZW–ZZ: birds (female heterogametic) · Haplo-diploid: honey bee (drones haploid)

Disorders
Haemophilia + colour blindness: X-linked recessive · Sickle-cell: point mutation, Glu → Val (β-chain, chromosome 11), codons GAG → GUG
Down syndrome: trisomy 21 · Turner: 45, XO · Klinefelter: 47, XXY · Thalassemia: quantitative globin-chain defect (α — chromosome 16; β — chromosome 11)
Phenylketonuria: autosomal recessive, enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase missing

capsules.subject: NCERT Quick Notes
capsules.title: NCERT Quick Notes — Genetics II: Molecular Basis of Inheritance
capsules.body:
DNA facts
B-DNA: one turn = 3.4 nm, 10 bp, rise 0.34 nm/bp · Chargaff: A = T, G ≡ C · DNA diameter 2 nm
Meselson–Stahl (1958): semi-conservative replication, ¹⁵N + CsCl gradient in E. coli
Griffith transforming principle (1928); Avery–MacLeod–McCarty (biochemical nature); Hershey–Chase (1952, T₂ phage, ³²P/³⁵S)
DNA polymerase extends only 5′→3′; Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand joined by ligase · Origin of replication + replication fork

Expression
Central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein (Crick) · Reverse transcriptase in retroviruses (Temin & Baltimore)
Genetic code: triplet, degenerate, unambiguous, near-universal · AUG = start + methionine · Stop: UAA, UAG, UGA
Split genes: exons + introns; capping (5′), tailing (poly-A, 3′), splicing in eukaryotes
Lac operon: i (repressor) — p — o — z (β-galactosidase), y (permease), a (transacetylase); lactose = inducer
Human Genome Project: ≈ 3 billion bp, ~30,000 genes (initial estimate), chromosome 1 has most genes (2968), Y the fewest (231)

capsules.subject: NCERT Quick Notes
capsules.title: NCERT Quick Notes — Ecology: Populations, Ecosystems, Biodiversity
capsules.body:
Populations
Natality/immigration raise density; mortality/emigration lower it · Logistic growth: dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K — starts exponential, flattens at carrying capacity K
Age pyramids: triangular = expanding, bell = stable, urn = declining · Predator–prey and competition (Gause’s principle: complete competitors cannot coexist)

Ecosystem
10% law (Lindeman): only ~10% energy crosses each trophic level · GPP − R = NPP
Pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright · Decomposition: fragmentation → leaching → catabolism → humification → mineralisation
Ecological succession: hydrarch (water → forest) and xerarch (rock → forest); pioneer species: lichens on rock, phytoplankton in water

Biodiversity
Robert May’s global estimate ≈ 7 million species; >70% of recorded species are animals, insects the largest group (>70% of animals)
Species–area: log S = log C + Z log A (Z ≈ 0.1–0.2; for frugivorous birds/mammals in tropics ≈ 1.15)
“Evil Quartet” of loss: habitat loss, over-exploitation, alien-species invasion (Nile perch → cichlids; water hyacinth; Lantana), co-extinction
Rivet-popper hypothesis (Paul Ehrlich) · Broadly utilitarian, narrowly utilitarian and ethical arguments for conservation

capsules.subject: NCERT Quick Notes
capsules.title: NCERT Quick Notes — Cell Biology: Cell Cycle & Biomolecules
capsules.body:
Cell cycle
Interphase ≈ 95% of cycle: G₁ (growth) → S (DNA doubles; centrosome duplicates in animals) → G₂ · M phase often under an hour in human cells (~24 h cycle)
Prophase: condensation · Metaphase: metaphase plate, spindle check · Anaphase: sister chromatids split (centromere divides) · Telophase + cytokinesis (cell plate in plants, furrow in animals)
Meiosis: prophase I — leptotene, zygotene (synapsis, bivalent), pachytene (crossing over, recombinase), diplotene (chiasmata visible), diakinesis
Significance of meiosis: variation + constant chromosome number across generations; mitosis = growth, repair, asexual reproduction

Biomolecules & enzymes
Most abundant animal protein: collagen; most abundant protein on Earth: RuBisCO
Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised by the body · Lipids are NOT true polymers
Enzymes: lower activation energy; competitive inhibitor resembles substrate (e.g., malonate vs succinate dehydrogenase); feedback inhibition — allosteric
Co-factors: prosthetic group (tightly bound organic), coenzyme (loose; NAD/NADP from niacin), metal ions (Zn²⁺ for carboxypeptidase; Mg²⁺ for kinases)

capsules.subject: NEET Updates
capsules.title: No NEET 2027 notification yet — trust only neet.nta.nic.in
capsules.body:
Read this before believing any “NEET 2027 notification out” post. As of late October 2026, NTA has not released the NEET-UG 2027 bulletin. Some websites are claiming a notification was released on 13 October with applications closing 15 November — those claims contradict every other source and are not supported by nta.ac.in or neet.nta.nic.in.

What is actually known: the 2027 application window is expected around February 2027 with the exam around May 2027, following the usual NTA cycle. Whether NEET-UG moves to a computer-based test (CBT) is still only “under consideration” — no decision has been announced.

Your rule: treat any date, fee or format claim as false until it appears on neet.nta.nic.in. When the real bulletin drops, this page will carry it as an alert the same day.

capsules.subject: General
capsules.title: NEET 2027: don't trust the date rumours (24 Oct 2026)
capsules.body: Third-party sites are claiming the NEET 2027 notification was released on 13/23 October 2026 with the exam on 3 May 2027 — but as of 18 October 2026, NTA had NOT officially confirmed any 2027 dates; registration windows and schedules circulating online are unverified. Verify everything at neet.nta.nic.in only, and keep Class 12 documents, photos and signatures ready for the real bulletin.

capsules.subject: Physics
capsules.title: Atomic clocks keep NavIC ticking (science in news)
capsules.body: NavIC stopped giving location data partly because of atomic-clock failures on satellites. Exam angle: satellite navigation needs clocks accurate to nanoseconds — a 1-microsecond error means ~300 m position error (c = 3×108 m/s). Caesium/rubidium atomic clocks use the hyperfine transition frequency as the time standard; GPS, Galileo and NavIC all depend on them. NVS-03 (30 Oct 2026) aims to restore NavIC's 4-satellite minimum.

capsules.subject: Physics
capsules.title: Orbital decay: why SpaDex re-entered (science in news)
capsules.body: SpaDex-A/B re-entered the atmosphere on 12-13 Oct 2026 after ~22 months. Exam angle: in low Earth orbit, atmospheric drag — even at ~400-500 km — bleeds orbital energy; once fuel was exhausted, the orbits decayed progressively. Re-entry heating comes from adiabatic compression of air ahead of the vehicle, not 'friction' alone. The mission had demonstrated autonomous rendezvous and docking in 2025.

capsules.subject: Current affairs
capsules.title: NEET-UG two-tier proposal and NTA accountability (October 2026)
capsules.body: A parliamentary committee report of 11 October 2026 advised the National Testing Agency to restructure NEET-UG, which serves over 22 lakh candidates for MBBS, BDS, nursing and AYUSH seats, into a two-tier model: a unified preliminary test and course-specific mains. It also urged a formal statutory framework making the NTA directly accountable to Parliament. Aspirants should note the status: a committee recommendation, not an NTA notification; current preparation should follow the existing single-stage pattern until the NTA announces otherwise.

capsules.subject: Biology in News
capsules.title: Nobel Prize in Medicine 2026
capsules.body: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel, announced in the Nobel week of 5–12 October 2026. For NEET revision, connect the prize to the syllabus themes of neural signalling and light-sensitive proteins, and note the laureates' surnames for current-affairs-linked biology questions.

capsules.subject: Exam Updates
capsules.title: NTA plans AI helpline and coordinated 2027 exam dates
capsules.body: In October 2026 the NTA said it would roll out an AI-powered helpline for candidates of exams including NEET UG and JEE Main, repurposing toll-free number 1800 180 47 47, to cut delays in answering application queries. The agency also plans to align JEE Main 2027 Session 2 dates with NEET and CUET so candidates can manage multiple high-stakes exams in the spring season. Verified: 25 October 2026.

capsules.subject: Biology
capsules.title: Optogenetics: how light switches nerve cells
capsules.body: Optogenetics, recognised by the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, rests on channelrhodopsin — a light-gated ion channel protein found in a single-celled alga. When light of the right wavelength hits it, the channel opens and ions flow, switching the nerve cell on or off. Researchers use this to map neural circuits and, experimentally, to restore light sensitivity in vision loss.

capsules.subject: Biology
capsules.title: Nobel Medicine 2026: light as a switch for nerve cells
capsules.body: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. Certain microbial proteins form ion channels that open when struck by light; inserting these proteins into nerve cells lets researchers control those cells with flashes of light and investigate how circuits drive behaviour. The technique is now a standard tool in neuroscience.

capsules.subject: Exams
capsules.title: NTA's new candidate helpline: what it is and what it is not (27 October 2026)
capsules.body: NTA launched a 24x7 toll-free helpline, 1800-180-4747, currently being trialled, alongside a helpdesk at 011-69227700 operating 8 am to 10 pm daily. NTA cautioned that its official helplines would never ask for passwords or one-time passwords — any such request is a fraud signal.

capsules.subject: Biology
capsules.title: Optogenetics: switching nerve cells with light
capsules.body: Optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins such as channelrhodopsin to switch individual nerve cells on or off in a living brain. The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine recognised the discoveries that made this possible. Applications under research include mapping neural circuits behind memory and behaviour and work towards restoring sight in people with visual impairment.

capsules.subject: Biology
capsules.title: NEET-UG: no date announced in the revised NTA calendar
capsules.body: The NTA's revised examination calendar published 26 October 2026 reordered UGC NET, Joint CSIR-UGC NET, JEE Main and CUET PG dates, but stated that the NEET-UG date had not yet been announced. The NTA said dates in the calendar are tentative and may change for administrative, academic, statutory or logistical reasons.

capsules.subject: Counselling
capsules.title: UP NEET Round 3 schedule released (27 October 2026)
capsules.body: The Directorate General of Medical Education and Training, Uttar Pradesh, released the schedule for the third round of UP NEET UG 2026 online counselling: registration from 26 October (5 pm) to 28 October (2 pm), fee deposit to 28 October (3 pm), merit list on 28 October, choice filling from 28 October (5 pm) to 31 October (5 pm), allotment result on 2 November, and allotment letters and admission from 3 to 7 November 2026.

capsules.subject: Counselling
capsules.title: MCC debunks fake cut-off percentile notice (13 October 2026)
capsules.body: The Medical Counselling Committee clarified on 13 October 2026 that a notice circulating in the public domain, claiming a reduction of the percentile in NEET UG Counselling 2026, was fake and that no such decision had been taken by the competent authority. MCC reiterated that it hosts no website other than www.mcc.nic.in and asked candidates to report fraudulent websites or agents.

capsules.subject: Biology
capsules.title: Medicine price caps reach the Supreme Court (27 October 2026)
capsules.body: The Supreme Court reserved its verdict on a PIL seeking caps on essential drug prices, after observing that a chemotherapy injection billed at Rs 1,30,000 against a dealer price of Rs 11,000 reflected mark-ups of up to 1,000%. The Centre said the trade margin on cancer drugs was capped at 30% of MRP; the bench noted about 90% of medicines remain outside the Drug Price Control Order and Ayushman Bharat cover is capped at Rs 5 lakh.

capsules.subject: Chemistry
capsules.title: Nobel Chemistry 2026: Kagan and Soai on homochirality
capsules.body: Henri B. Kagan (France) and Kenso Soai (Japan) won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Kagan showed that a small enantiomeric imbalance could be amplified far beyond linear expectation; Soai built the first asymmetric autocatalytic reaction, in which the product catalyses its own formation and amplifies chirality. The work bears on the century-old question of how life came to use one mirror-image form, and on synthesising single-enantiomer pharmaceuticals, since more than half of clinically used drugs are chiral.

capsules.subject: Biology
capsules.title: New electric ray: Tetronarce ramanamurthyi (October 2026)
capsules.body: Scientists of the Zoological Survey of India, led by K. K. Bineesh and Anil Kasinath with David A. Ebert of San Jose State University, described the Arabian Black Electric Ray from the south-eastern Arabian Sea. The species honours M. V. Ramana Murthy, Mission Director of the Deep Ocean Mission. Distinguishing features include the uniform dark upper surface, large spiracles and endolymphatic pores, a distinctive mouth-to-nostril ratio, and small electric organs. For NEET: remember genus Tetronarce, family Torpedinidae, class Chondrichthyes.

capsules.subject: Biology
capsules.title: New electric ray: how a species is established
capsules.body: 27 October 2026 — ZSI scientists K. K. Bineesh and Anil Kasinath, with David A. Ebert, described Tetronarce ramanamurthyi from nine Arabian Sea specimens using anatomy (dark upper surface, disc wider than long, no fleshy projections around spiracles) and DNA sequencing; the paper appeared in Zootaxa.

capsules.subject: Environment
capsules.title: India's biodiversity numbers at COP-17
capsules.body: 27 October 2026 — India reported 1,134 Protected Areas, 103 Ramsar sites, 57 Biodiversity Heritage Sites and 18 Biosphere Reserves (13 in UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Network), and 23 National Biodiversity Targets with 142 indicators under its updated NBSAP.

capsules.subject: Biology
capsules.title: Optogenetics: the 2026 Medicine Nobel in brief
capsules.body: Optogenetics uses light-sensitive ion channels — proteins that open in response to light — to control and investigate cellular activity, especially in neurons. The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine recognised Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries concerning these light-gated ion channels. In practice, a light-sensitive channel gene is expressed in target cells, so flashes of light can switch those cells on or off with millisecond precision, letting researchers map brain circuits and test causal roles of specific neurons.

capsules.subject: Biology
capsules.title: Optogenetics: switching brain cells with light
capsules.body: Optogenetics, recognised by the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, combines genetics and optics: light-gated ion channels — channel proteins that open in response to light — are introduced into specific nerve cells. A pulse of light can then activate or silence just those cells in a living brain, with split-second timing, revealing cause-and-effect links between circuits, behaviour and disease. The approach has reshaped basic brain science and is being tested in animal models of blindness, Parkinson's disease and depression, although clinical use in humans remains at an early stage. The laureates are Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.

capsules.subject: Environment
capsules.title: Floods and public health: lessons from Cyclone Arnab and the Sankosh alert
capsules.body: Cyclone Arnab and the Bhutan GLOF together illustrate the health consequences of flooding that NEET aspirants must connect to biology: stagnant water breeds mosquitoes that transmit dengue and malaria; contaminated water spreads cholera, typhoid and hepatitis; and disrupted services endanger pregnant women, infants and chronic-disease patients. Andhra Pradesh's pre-emptive shifting of 3,100 pregnant women, with 367 deliveries in hospitals, shows preparedness reducing maternal and neonatal risk. Post-flood priorities are safe water, sanitation, vector control, vaccination where indicated, and disease surveillance — all grounded in microbiology, ecology and human physiology.

capsules.subject: Physics
capsules.title: Atomic clocks and satellite navigation: the science behind NVS-03
capsules.body: Satellite navigation depends on extremely precise timekeeping: a timing error of one microsecond translates into a positioning error of about 300 metres. NVS-03 carries an indigenous rubidium atomic clock, which uses the stable hyperfine transition frequency of rubidium atoms, alongside procured clocks for redundancy. The satellite joins a constellation that must maintain at least four visible satellites for standalone positioning. Its L1, L5 and S-band signals let receivers correct ionospheric delays. The GSLV-F18 launch to Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit demonstrates the physics of orbital mechanics, from launch energy to orbit-raising with onboard thrusters.

capsules.subject: Examinations
capsules.title: NTA reform: question bank, CBT and accountability (Oct 2026)
capsules.body: October 2026 — The parliamentary standing committee on education's report 'Reforms and Strengthening of NTA', presented on 9 October 2026, recommended a large, diverse, continuously updated question bank, a phased move to computer-based testing including for NEET-UG, reliance on experts from IITs, AIIMSs and IIMs for question banks and translation, fee transparency and student-safety rules for coaching centres, and a parliamentary framework ensuring NTA's accountability to Parliament.

capsules.subject: Space
capsules.title: Why atomic clocks matter for navigation (31 Oct 2026)
capsules.body: 31 October 2026 — NVS-03 placed a third indigenous atomic clock in orbit. Satellite navigation depends on extremely precise timing: each satellite's atomic clock lets receivers measure signal travel times, and the indigenous rubidium clock reduces dependence on procured clocks for NavIC's positioning, navigation and timing services.

oneliners.text: Distance is the scalar length of the path travelled; displacement is the vector change in position and its magnitude never exceeds the distance.
Average velocity equals total displacement divided by total time, while average speed equals total distance divided by total time.
The distance travelled in the nth second of uniformly accelerated motion is u + a(2n-1)/2.
In projectile motion the horizontal velocity component stays constant while the vertical component changes uniformly under gravity.
Projectile range R = u² sin2θ/g is maximum at 45 degrees, and complementary angles of projection give the same range.
At the peak of its trajectory a projectile's velocity is entirely horizontal.
A passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes suddenly because of inertia of motion.
A gun recoils on firing because the total momentum of the isolated gun-bullet system is conserved.
Impulse equals the change in momentum (J = F·dt = dp); cricketers pull their hands back while catching to lengthen dt and reduce force.
We walk forward because static friction pushes us ahead as our feet push backward on the ground.
Static friction self-adjusts up to a maximum fₛ = μₛ·N, while kinetic friction fₖ = μₖ·N with μₖ smaller than μₛ.
Centripetal force mv²/r always points toward the centre of the circular path; centrifugal force is only a pseudo-force in rotating frames.
Work W = F·s·cos(θ) is zero whenever the applied force is perpendicular to the displacement.
The area under a force-displacement graph equals the work done by that force.
Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is mgh; elastic potential energy stored in a spring is (1/2)kx².
Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t = F·v, and one kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 × 10⁶ joules.
In an elastic collision between identical masses with one initially at rest, the two bodies move off at 90 degrees to each other.
The coefficient of restitution is 1 for a perfectly elastic collision and 0 for a perfectly inelastic one.
Torque is the rotational analogue of force, τ = r x F, and the rotational form of Newton's second law is τ = I·α.
The radius of gyration K is defined by I = MK²; mass farther from the axis gives larger K.
A diver tucks in mid-air to shrink the moment of inertia and spin faster, conserving angular momentum.
A solid sphere beats a hollow sphere down an incline because its smaller moment of inertia gives larger acceleration.
The centre of mass of a uniform rod lies at its midpoint and that of a uniform ring or disc at its geometric centre.
The universal gravitation constant G is 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg², and g = GM/R² at Earth's surface.
Acceleration due to gravity falls with depth as g(1 - h/R) and with small heights as approximately g(1 - 2h/R).
Orbital velocity is vₒ = √(GM/r) while escape velocity is vₑ = √(2GM/R), about 11.2 km/s for Earth.
Kepler's third law states that the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its orbital radius.
A geostationary satellite has a 24-hour period and stays about 35,800 km above the equator in the equatorial plane.
Steel has a larger Young's modulus than rubber, so steel is more elastic than rubber despite rubber stretching more.
Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain in a stretched wire.
Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every portion of the fluid.
The continuity equation A1·v1 = A2·v2 means a fluid speeds up wherever the pipe narrows.
Bernoulli's principle says P + (1/2)ρ·v² + ρ·g·h stays constant along a streamline, so fast-moving air exerts lower pressure.
Torricelli's law gives the speed of efflux as v = √(2gh), the same as free fall from height h.
Stokes' law states the viscous drag on a sphere is F = 6·π·eta·r·v; terminal velocity is reached when drag plus buoyancy balance weight.
Capillary rise is given by h = 2S·cos(θ)/(r·ρ·g), so narrower tubes lift liquids higher.
The angle of contact is acute for water on glass but obtuse for mercury on glass.
For thermal expansion, the area coefficient is twice and the volume coefficient three times the linear coefficient α.
Water's specific heat capacity, 4186 J/kg/K, is the highest among common liquids and moderates coastal climates.
Latent heat produces no temperature change during a phase change; steam scalds worse than boiling water because of its latent heat.
Newton's law of cooling states the rate of heat loss is proportional to the temperature difference for small differences.
Wien's displacement law, λₘ·T = 2.89 × 10⁻³ m·K, means hotter bodies radiate maximally at shorter wavelengths.
By the Stefan-Boltzmann law radiated power E = σ·T⁴, so doubling absolute temperature raises radiation sixteen-fold.
A black body is a perfect absorber and emitter; Kirchhoff's law links a body's emissivity to its absorptivity.
The ideal gas equation PV = nRT combines Boyle's, Charles's and Gay-Lussac's laws.
Graham's law: a gas's rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass.
A monatomic gas has 3 degrees of freedom and a diatomic gas 5 at room temperature, each contributing (1/2)kT by equipartition.
Mayer's relation gives Cp - Cv = R; γ is 5/3 for monatomic and 7/5 for diatomic gases.
The first law of thermodynamics is dQ = dU + dW; in an isothermal change dU = 0 so all heat becomes work.
For an adiabatic change PV^γ = constant and TV^(γ-1) = constant, with no heat exchanged.
Carnot efficiency eta = 1 - T2/T1 on the Kelvin scale is the maximum possible between two reservoirs.
In simple harmonic motion velocity is maximum at the mean position and zero at the extremes, while acceleration is maximum at the extremes.
The total mechanical energy of an SHM oscillator is (1/2)kA², constant and proportional to the square of the amplitude.
In SHM the velocity leads displacement by 90 degrees, and acceleration leads displacement by 180 degrees.
A seconds pendulum has a two-second period and a length of about one metre.
Resonance occurs when a system is driven at its natural frequency and oscillates with maximum amplitude.
Wave speed v = f·λ, and the intensity of a wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude.
When two nearly equal frequencies superpose, the beat frequency heard is the difference of the two frequencies.
In the Doppler effect the apparent frequency rises as source and observer approach and falls as they recede.
In a standing wave the nodes stay at zero displacement, antinodes oscillate maximally, and consecutive nodes are λ/2 apart.
The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is f = (1/2l)·√(T/μ).
An open organ pipe sounds all harmonics while a closed pipe sounds only the odd harmonics.
Coulomb's law F = k·q1·q2/r² uses k = 9 × 10⁹ N m²/C² in free space.
The electric field of a point charge is E = kq/r² (vector) while its potential V = kq/r is a scalar.
An electric dipole has moment p = q·(2a); in a uniform field it experiences torque τ = pE·sin(θ).
Gauss's law: the total electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀.
The field of an infinite charged sheet is σ/2·ε₀, but just outside a charged conductor it is σ/ε₀.
A parallel-plate capacitor has C = ε₀·A/d; inserting a dielectric of constant K multiplies capacitance by K.
Capacitors in series combine as 1/C = sum(1/Ci) and in parallel as C = sum(Ci), the reverse of resistor rules.
Energy stored in a charged capacitor is U = (1/2)CV² = Q²/2C.
Drift velocity vᵈ = I/(n·e·A) is only millimetres per second, while electrons' random thermal speed is about 10⁵ m/s.
Resistivity ρ = R·A/l is a material property; metals' resistance rises with temperature while semiconductors' falls.
No current flows through the galvanometer when a Wheatstone bridge is balanced.
A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when P/Q = R/S; the metre bridge works on this null-point principle.
A potentiometer measures EMF without drawing current, so it gives the true EMF unlike an ordinary voltmeter.
A cell's internal resistance is r = (E - V)/I, and terminal voltage falls as more current is drawn.
Joule's heating law gives H = I²·R·t; electric power can be written P = VI = I²·R = V²/R.
The Biot-Savart law gives dB = (μ₀/4π)·I·dl·sin(θ)/r²; at the centre of a circular loop B = μ₀·I/2R.
The field of a long straight wire is B = μ₀·I/2·π·r, and inside a long solenoid it is uniform at B = μ₀·n·I.
The Lorentz force F = qvB·sin(θ) bends a charge moving perpendicular to B into a circle of radius mv/qB.
A cyclotron uses crossed electric and magnetic fields to accelerate charges, with orbital frequency f = qB/2·π·m.
The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is F = B·I·l·sin(θ); parallel currents attract and antiparallel ones repel.
A galvanometer is converted to an ammeter with a low shunt in parallel and to a voltmeter with a high resistance in series.
The angle of dip of Earth's magnetic field is zero at the magnetic equator and 90 degrees at the magnetic poles.
Diamagnetic substances are weakly repelled by a magnet, paramagnetic weakly attracted, and ferromagnetic strongly attracted.
Above the Curie temperature a ferromagnetic material loses its permanent magnetism and becomes paramagnetic.
Faraday's law gives induced EMF ε = -d(φ)/dt; Lenz's law explains the minus sign as opposition to the change.
A rod of length l moving at speed v perpendicular to field B develops a motional EMF ε = B·l·v.
In AC circuits Iᵣms = I₀/√(2) and Vᵣms = V₀/√(2); the 220 V mains supply is an rms value.
Inductive reactance X_L = ω·L grows with frequency while capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(ω·C) falls with frequency.
The quality factor Q = ω₀·L/R measures how sharp the resonance is in a series LCR circuit.
Average power in a purely inductive or capacitive AC circuit is zero, giving wattless current; power factor is cos(φ) = R/Z.
A transformer works only on AC by mutual induction, stepping voltage up or down with current changing inversely.
Snell's law n1·sin(i) = n2·sin(r) governs refraction at an interface between two media.
A glass slab displaces a light ray laterally without changing its direction; the lateral shift grows with slab thickness.
The lensmaker's formula 1/f = (n-1)(1/R1 - 1/R2) gives lens power P = 100/f with f in centimetres (dioptre).
A convex mirror always forms an erect, diminished virtual image whatever the object distance.
At minimum deviation a prism ray passes symmetrically, and the material's index is n = sin((A + δₘ)/2)/sin(A/2).
A compound microscope magnifies about (L/fₒ)(1 + D/fₑ); an astronomical telescope about -fₒ/fₑ in normal adjustment.
Wavefronts from a point source are spherical, and Huygens' principle treats every wavefront point as a source of secondary wavelets.
J.J. Thomson discovered the electron via cathode rays, Goldstein discovered the proton via anode rays, and Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.
Rutherford's α-scattering experiment showed the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny dense positive nucleus.
An s-orbital is spherical, p-orbitals are dumbbell-shaped, and d-orbitals are mostly double-dumbbell in shape.
The (n + l) rule fills 4s before 3d because 4 + 0 is less than 3 + 2.
The de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle mark the limits of Bohr's fixed orbits.
Isotopes share proton number but differ in neutrons, isobars share mass number, and isotones share neutron number.
Moseley restated the periodic law in terms of atomic number, and the modern table has 7 periods and 18 groups.
The diagonal relationship makes lithium resemble magnesium and beryllium resemble aluminium in properties.
Lanthanide contraction, caused by poor shielding of 4f electrons, makes 4d and 5d elements nearly equal in size.
Inert pair effect makes the +1 state stable for thallium and +2 for lead among heavier p-block elements.
Second-period elements show anomalous behaviour due to small size, high electronegativity and absence of d-orbitals.
Noble gases have the highest ionisation enthalpies and near-zero electron gain enthalpies in their periods.
Fajan's rules: small highly charged cations polarise anions strongly, giving covalent character to ionic compounds.
Carbon's s-character rises 25% (sp3) < 33% (sp2) < 50% (sp), making sp-hybridised carbon the most electronegative.
Sigma bonds form by head-on overlap and are stronger; π bonds form by sideways overlap and restrict rotation.
Molecular orbital theory always produces exactly as many molecular orbitals as the atomic orbitals combined.
Molecular orbital theory explains oxygen's paramagnetism through two unpaired electrons in its π-star 2p orbitals.
Hydrogen bonding in HF, H2O and NH3 arises from H bonded to small highly electronegative N, O or F atoms.
Standard enthalpy of formation of every element in its most stable form is taken as zero.
Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction of a reversible reaction.
The common ion effect suppresses the ionisation of a weak electrolyte, lowering solubilities of sparingly soluble salts.
Fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent and lithium the strongest reducing agent in the electrochemical series.
Protium, deuterium and tritium are hydrogen's isotopes; tritium is radioactive while the other two are stable.
Hydrogen peroxide has a non-planar open-book structure with a dihedral angle near 90 degrees in the gas phase.
Alkali metals are soft, low-melting and the most reactive metals; they are stored under kerosene.
Flame colours: lithium crimson, sodium golden yellow, potassium lilac, calcium brick red, strontium crimson, barium apple green.
Beryllium and magnesium give no flame colour because their electrons need too much energy to excite.
Plaster of Paris is CaSO4.(1/2)H2O, gypsum is CaSO4.2H2O, washing soda is Na2CO3.10H2O and baking soda is NaHCO3.
Carbon shows catenation most strongly due to strong C-C bonds; silicon shows it far less.
Carbon monoxide is a neutral, poisonous gas that binds haemoglobin; carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide.
Ammonia is made by Haber's process: N2 + 3H2 over iron at about 200 atm and 700 K.
Nitric acid is made by Ostwald's process: catalytic oxidation of ammonia over platinum-rhodium gauze.
Sulphuric acid is made by the Contact process: oxidation of SO2 to SO3 over V2O5 catalyst.
Oleum is fuming sulphuric acid, H2S2O7, made by dissolving SO3 in concentrated H2SO4.
Interhalogen compounds like ClF3 and IF7 are stronger halogenating agents than the halogens themselves.
Xenon forms XeF2 (linear), XeF4 (square planar) and XeF6 (distorted octahedral) under special conditions.
Helium's lightness and inertness suit it for balloons and for diluting oxygen in divers' breathing mixtures.
Transition metals show variable oxidation states, form coloured ions, are paramagnetic and act as catalysts.
Potassium dichromate is orange and potassium permanganate is purple; both are strong oxidising agents in acid.
In acidic medium dichromate reduces to green Cr3+ and permanganate reduces to colourless Mn2+.
Actinides are all radioactive and show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanides.
Werner's theory distinguishes ionisable counter ions from non-ionisable ligands inside the coordination sphere.
EDTA is a hexadentate ligand; ethylenediamine and oxalate are bidentate, and chelation greatly raises complex stability.
Linkage isomerism appears with ambidentate ligands like NO2(-)/ONO(-); ionisation isomerism exchanges counter ion and ligand.
Geometrical isomerism needs cis-trans arrangements, possible in square planar MA2B2 and octahedral MA4B2 complexes.
The spectrochemical series orders ligands I- < Br- < Cl- < F- < OH- < H2O < NH3 < en < CN- < CO by field strength.
Strong-field ligands give low-spin complexes with maximum pairing; weak-field ligands give high-spin complexes.
The colour of coordination compounds comes from d-d electronic transitions between split t2g and eg orbitals.
CFSE measures the extra stability from d-orbital splitting; octahedral splitting δₒ exceeds tetrahedral δₜ.
Homolytic fission gives free radicals, heterolytic fission gives carbocations and carbanions.
Carbocation stability follows 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg; carbanion stability follows the reverse order.
Resonance delocalises π electrons and stabilises molecules; the -I effect withdraws electrons through σ bonds.
Hyperconjugation from adjacent C-H σ bonds stabilises carbocations and alkenes.
Aromaticity needs a cyclic planar conjugated system with (4n+2) π electrons by Huckel's rule.
Lassaigne's test detects nitrogen as Prussian blue, sulphur as black lead sulphide, and halogens as silver halide precipitates.
Kjeldahl's method cannot estimate nitrogen in nitro, azo or diazo compounds because they do not give ammonium sulphate.
Free-radical chlorination of alkanes attacks C-H bonds in the order 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg.
In ethane the staggered conformation is more stable than the eclipsed due to torsional strain.
Oxymercuration-demercuration hydrates alkenes by Markovnikov's rule with no carbocation rearrangement.
Ozonolysis cleaves alkenes at the double bond, locating its position from the carbonyl products.
Terminal alkynes are acidic enough to give precipitates with ammoniacal AgNO3 and Cu2Cl2.
Nitration of benzene uses concentrated HNO3 with concentrated H2SO4, generating the nitronium ion electrophile.
Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation need anhydrous AlCl3 and fail with strongly deactivating groups on the ring.
-OH, -NH2, -CH3 and halogens direct ortho-para; -NO2, -CN, -CHO and -COOH direct meta in electrophilic substitution.
Aryl halides are far less reactive than alkyl halides toward nucleophilic substitution because of resonance stabilisation.
Saytzeff's rule: dehydrohalogenation gives the more substituted alkene as the major product.
Grignard reagents RMgX are made in dry ether and are destroyed instantly by water or alcohols.
Lucas reagent (ZnCl2 + conc. HCl) turns 3 deg alcohols turbid at once, 2 deg within five minutes, and leaves 1 deg clear at room temperature.
Acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols follows the ease 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg via carbocation intermediates.
Phenol is more acidic than alcohols because its phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised.
The Reimer-Tiemann reaction converts phenol with CHCl3/NaOH into salicylaldehyde.
Kolbe's reaction carboxylates sodium phenoxide with CO2 to give salicylic acid.
Williamson synthesis builds ethers from an alkyl halide and a sodium alkoxide.
The iodoform test is positive for compounds containing CH3CO- or CH3CH(OH)- groups.
Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes; Fehling's solution gives a red Cu2O precipitate with aldehydes.
Aldol condensation needs α-hydrogens and dilute NaOH; Cannizzaro needs aldehydes without α-hydrogens and concentrated KOH.
Clemmensen reduction (Zn-Hg/conc. HCl) and Wolff-Kishner reduction (NH2NH2/KOH) both convert C=O into CH2.
Rosenmund reduction turns acyl chlorides into aldehydes with H2 over Pd-BaSO4.
Stephen reduction converts alkyl nitriles into aldehydes with SnCl2 and HCl.
Etard reaction oxidises toluene to benzaldehyde with chromyl chloride CrO2Cl2.
Carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols; electron-withdrawing groups strengthen them further.
The Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction α-halogenates carboxylic acids with Br2 and red phosphorus.
In aqueous solution aliphatic amine basicity follows 2 deg > 1 deg > 3 deg, and aniline is weaker than ammonia.
Diazotisation of aromatic primary amines uses NaNO2/HCl at 0-5 C to form diazonium salts.
Sandmeyer reaction replaces the diazo group with Cl, Br or CN using cuprous salts.
The carbylamine test gives a foul-smelling isocyanide only with primary amines, using CHCl3 and alcoholic KOH.
Hoffmann bromamide degradation shortens an amide by one carbon to give a primary amine with Br2/KOH.
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis prepares pure primary amines without over-alkylation.
A maximum-boiling azeotrope such as 68% nitric acid shows large negative deviation from Raoult's law.
The van't Hoff factor i is the observed colligative property divided by the calculated value, correcting for dissociation or association.
Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, never on their chemical identity.
Molality stays constant when temperature changes, which is why it is preferred over molarity in thermodynamic work.
Applying pressure above the osmotic pressure reverses osmosis; this is how sea water is desalinated.
In a galvanic cell the anode is negative and the cathode is positive; in an electrolytic cell the signs reverse.
Faraday's first law of electrolysis states W = ZQ, where Z equals equivalent mass divided by 96500.
A zero-order reaction has half-life t1/2 = [R]0/2k, which shortens as reactant is consumed.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy and is regenerated at the end.
Iron rusts only when both air and moisture are present; coating it with zinc protects it sacrificially.
A 12 V lead-storage battery contains six 2 V cells; a Leclanche dry cell gives 1.5 V.
Specific conductivity decreases on dilution while molar conductivity increases.
The nucleolus synthesises ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits; it disappears during prophase and reforms in telophase.
Mycoplasma (PPLO) is the smallest known cell, while the ostrich egg is the largest single cell.
Centrioles show a 9+0 microtubule arrangement, while cilia and flagella show a 9+2 arrangement.
Interphase is the longest phase of the cell cycle, and DNA replication occurs during the S phase.
Colchicine arrests dividing cells at metaphase by preventing spindle fibre formation.
The short interphase between meiosis I and meiosis II is called interkinesis, and no DNA replication occurs in it.
Mitosis yields two identical diploid cells, while meiosis halves the chromosome number and generates variation.
Emil Fischer proposed the lock-and-key model of enzyme action; ribozymes are catalytic RNA molecules.
Non-competitive inhibitors lower an enzyme's Vmax without changing its Km.
The DNA double helix has antiparallel strands with adenine pairing thymine and guanine pairing cytosine.
Chlorophyceae possess chlorophyll a and b and store starch; Chlamydomonas, Volvox and Spirogyra belong here.
Agar from Gelidium and Gracilaria is used to culture microbes, while algin is obtained from brown algae.
Pteridophytes are the first vascular land plants; heterospory in Selaginella foreshadows the seed habit.
Cycas bears coralloid roots housing nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, while Pinus roots associate with mycorrhizal fungi.
Poriferans possess a canal system and choanocytes; Sycon, Spongilla and Euspongia are examples.
Cnidarians carry cnidoblasts with stinging nematocysts; Physalia is the Portuguese man-of-war.
Arthropoda is the largest phylum, with jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton; Limulus is a living fossil.
Echinoderms move with a water vascular system and show radial symmetry as adults; Asterias is a starfish.
Mammals are defined by mammary glands, hair, a diaphragm and external ears; Ornithorhynchus lays eggs.
Rhizophora produces pneumatophores, breathing roots with lenticels, for aeration in marshy soil.
Potato is a stem tuber bearing eyes, whereas sweet potato is a modified adventitious root.
Placentation is marginal in pea, axile in tomato, parietal in mustard, free central in Dianthus and basal in sunflower.
Vexillary aestivation characterises pea flowers, while valvate aestivation occurs in Calotropis.
Munch's mass flow hypothesis explains phloem transport of food from source to sink.
Plants require 17 essential elements: nine macronutrients and eight micronutrients including nickel.
Nitrogen deficiency causes chlorosis in older leaves first because nitrogen is a mobile element.
In nitrification, Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonia to nitrite and Nitrobacter oxidises nitrite to nitrate.
Denitrifying bacteria like Pseudomonas and Thiobacillus return nitrogen gas to the atmosphere.
Leghaemoglobin, the pink pigment of root nodules, shields nitrogenase from oxygen.
In the Z-scheme electrons flow from PS-II (P680) to PS-I (P700), and photolysis of water occurs at PS-II.
Non-cyclic photophosphorylation yields both ATP and NADPH, while cyclic photophosphorylation yields only ATP.
The Calvin cycle invests 18 ATP and 12 NADPH to fix six CO2 into one glucose; RuBisCO is Earth's most abundant enzyme.
C4 plants show Kranz anatomy: PEPcase first fixes CO2 in mesophyll cells and RuBisCO acts in bundle-sheath cells.
Photorespiration engages chloroplasts, peroxisomes and mitochondria but produces neither ATP nor NADPH.
Blackman's law of limiting factors says photosynthesis is capped by whichever factor is in shortest supply.
Glycolysis is also called the EMP pathway, after Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas.
The Krebs cycle operates in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing two CO2 per acetyl-CoA and generating GTP.
In alcoholic fermentation, pyruvate is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde and then reduced to ethanol, regenerating NAD+.
Auxin enforces apical dominance, and the synthetic auxin 2,4-D is used as a weedicide.
Abscisic acid closes stomata during water stress and is known as the stress hormone.
Cytokinins delay leaf senescence through the Richmond-Lang effect and promote cell division in tissue culture.
Garner and Allard discovered photoperiodism; vernalisation is the low-temperature promotion of flowering.
Salivary amylase (ptyalin) digests starch at pH 6.8, and lysozyme in saliva kills bacteria.
Stomach HCl activates pepsinogen into pepsin, maintains pH 1.8 and destroys ingested microbes.
Succus entericus finishes digestion with maltase, lactase, sucrase, dipeptidases, lipase and nucleosidases.
Tidal volume is 500 mL and vital capacity is roughly 3500 to 4500 mL in a healthy adult.
Roughly 70 percent of carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate ions, 20-25 percent as carbaminohaemoglobin and 7 percent dissolved.
In an ECG the P wave marks atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex ventricular depolarisation and the T wave ventricular repolarisation.
Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells at 60-65 percent and are actively phagocytic.
The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs all glucose and amino acids plus roughly 65 percent of the filtrate.
The counter-current mechanism of Henle's loop and vasa recta builds the medullary gradient from 300 to 1200 mOsm/L.
Huxley's sliding filament theory explains contraction; calcium ions expose myosin-binding sites on actin.
The adult human skeleton has 206 bones: 80 in the axial division and 126 in the appendicular division.
The resting membrane potential of a neuron is -70 mV, and the action potential peaks near +30 mV.
Saltatory conduction leaps between nodes of Ranvier, greatly speeding impulses in myelinated fibres.
Excess growth hormone causes gigantism in children and acromegaly in adults; its deficiency causes dwarfism.
Iodine deficiency causes goitre and cretinism, while Graves' disease produces exophthalmic goitre.
Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it; insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus.
The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline to mount fight-or-flight responses.
The Polygonum-type embryo sac is eight-nucleate and seven-celled.
Double fertilisation, the union of syngamy and triple fusion, was discovered by Nawaschin.
Coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm, and the endosperm of angiosperms is triploid.
Geitonogamy is genetically self-pollination but needs a pollinator; cleistogamous flowers never open.
Sertoli cells nourish developing sperm, while Leydig cells secrete testosterone.
Ovulation occurs near day 14 of the 28-day menstrual cycle, triggered by the LH surge.
The blastocyst implants into the uterine endometrium about seven days after fertilisation.
hCG secreted by the placenta is the hormone detected in pregnancy tests; oxytocin drives parturition.
Mendel tracked seven contrasting characters in garden pea plants.
Incomplete dominance in Mirabilis jalapa produces a 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation.
ABO blood groups display codominance and multiple alleles, giving six genotypes and four phenotypes.
Sickle-cell anaemia is a point mutation changing GAG to GUG, substituting valine for glutamate.
Griffith's 1928 transformation experiment used Streptococcus pneumoniae in mice.
Hershey and Chase labelled phage protein with 35S and DNA with 32P in the blender experiment.
Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli on 15N to prove DNA replication is semiconservative.
Darwin's finches on the Galapagos islands illustrate adaptive radiation from a common ancestor.
Homologous organs reveal divergent evolution, while analogous organs reveal convergent evolution.
Industrial melanism in the peppered moth Biston betularia is a classic case of natural selection.
Genetic drift changes allele frequencies by chance and hits hardest in small populations.
Homo habilis had a brain capacity of 650-800 cc, while Neanderthals reached about 1400 cc.
Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus, living about 15 million years ago, were the earliest known human ancestors.
Haemozoin, the toxic pigment released in malaria, triggers the characteristic chill and high fever.
Allergic responses are mediated by IgE antibodies through histamine and serotonin release.
Heroin (smack) is diacetylmorphine derived from poppy, and cocaine comes from Erythroxylum coca.
Cannabinoids from Cannabis sativa include marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja.
Hind II was the first restriction endonuclease characterised; EcoRI from E. coli RY13 cuts GAATTC leaving sticky ends.
The plasmid pBR322 carries ampicillin and tetracycline resistance markers along with ori and rop sequences.
Agrobacterium tumefaciens' Ti plasmid is the natural vector for introducing genes into plants.
PCR cycles through denaturation near 94 C, annealing near 54 C and extension at 72 C with Taq polymerase.
Bt cotton expresses cryIAc and cryIIAb proteins that kill cotton bollworms.
Golden rice is engineered to accumulate β-carotene, a vitamin A precursor.
Human insulin (Humulin) from Eli Lilly in 1983 was the first recombinant therapeutic protein.
The first gene therapy, in 1990, treated ADA deficiency in a four-year-old girl.
Gause's competitive exclusion principle holds that two species competing for one resource cannot stably coexist.
Lindeman proposed the 10 percent law for energy transfer between trophic levels.
Lichens pioneer primary succession on bare rock, while phytoplankton pioneer hydrarch succession.
Decomposition proceeds through fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation.
The species-area relationship log S = log C + Z log A uses Z values of 0.1-0.2 for small areas.
The evil quartet of biodiversity loss comprises habitat loss, over-exploitation, alien invasion and co-extinction.
In-situ conservation relies on national parks and biosphere reserves; ex-situ uses zoos and seed banks.
The Earth Summit met in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 and the World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg in 2002.
One electron-volt equals 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ joule.
The universal gas constant R is 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and Boltzmann's constant k is 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
Avogadro's number is 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
The charge of an electron is 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and its rest mass is 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
Planck's constant h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; the reduced constant ħ = h/2π.
The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 m/s (3 × 10⁸ m/s for calculations).
One atomic mass unit equals 931.5 MeV of energy.
The permittivity of free space ε₀ is 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻².
The permeability of free space μ₀ is 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
Gravitational constant G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
Escape velocity from Earth is about 11.2 km/s.
The value of g decreases with altitude and with depth below Earth's surface.
A geostationary satellite orbits at about 35,800 km above the equator with a 24-hour period.
Polar satellites orbit at roughly 800 km altitude in 84-minute periods.
Surface tension of water at room temperature is about 0.072 N/m.
The Reynolds number below ~1000 indicates laminar flow; above ~2000 the flow turns turbulent.
Bernoulli's principle: where a fluid's speed rises, its pressure falls.
Young's modulus of steel is about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa.
Poisson's ratio for most metals lies between 0.2 and 0.4.
The coefficient of linear expansion of a bimetallic strip's two metals must differ for it to bend on heating.
A Carnot engine's efficiency depends only on the source and sink temperatures: 1 − T₂/T₁.
Kelvin and Celsius scales differ by 273.15; a change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C.
Absolute zero (0 K = −273.15 °C) is unattainable by the third law of thermodynamics.
An adiabatic process has no heat exchange (Q = 0); an isothermal process keeps temperature constant.
The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q − W (physics sign convention: W is work done by the system).
The pH of a neutral solution is 7 at 25 °C; pH + pOH = 14 at this temperature.
The ionic product of water Kw is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
Faraday's constant is 96,485 C mol⁻¹.
Standard hydrogen electrode is assigned a potential of exactly 0.00 V.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element (3.98 on the Pauling scale).
Cesium is the most electropositive stable element.
The first ionisation enthalpy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Noble gases have the highest ionisation enthalpies in their periods.
Electron gain enthalpy is most negative for chlorine among all elements.
The common oxidation state of alkali metals is +1 and of alkaline earth metals is +2.
Diamond is sp³ hybridised; graphite layers are sp² hybridised.
The bond angle in methane is 109.5°, in ammonia 107°, and in water 104.5°.
VSEPR: lone pair–lone pair repulsion exceeds lone pair–bond pair, which exceeds bond pair–bond pair.
Hydrogen bonding is strongest in HF among the hydrogen halides.
Ice is less dense than liquid water because of its open hydrogen-bonded cage structure.
Water's maximum density occurs at 4 °C.
Heavy water D₂O has a molar mass of 20 g mol⁻¹.
The equivalent weight of KMnO₄ is M/5 in acidic medium and M/3 in alkaline medium.
Molarity depends on temperature (volume changes); molality does not.
An azeotrope boils at a constant temperature with fixed composition (e.g. 95.6% ethanol–water).
Raoult's law: the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component equals its mole fraction times its pure vapour pressure.
Elevation of boiling point and depression of freezing point are colligative properties depending only on solute particle count.
Osmotic pressure π = iCRT (van't Hoff equation).
The rate constant's units for a first-order reaction are s⁻¹; for second order, L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
A catalyst lowers activation energy without being consumed and cannot shift the equilibrium position.
Viruses were discovered by Ivanowsky (1892, TMV) and the term 'virus' was coined by Beijerinck.
Viroids are infectious RNA without a protein coat, discovered by T.O. Diener.
Prions are infectious misfolded proteins causing diseases like mad cow disease.
Lichens are symbiotic associations of algae (phycobiont) and fungi (mycobiont).
Mycorrhiza is the symbiotic association of fungi with plant roots, aiding mineral absorption.
Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in root nodules of legumes.
Frankia fixes nitrogen in root nodules of non-legumes like Alnus.
Anabaena in Azolla leaf cavities fixes nitrogen in paddy fields.
Cycas roots host nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria in coralloid roots.
Pinus roots form ectomycorrhizal association with fungi.
Double fertilisation (syngamy + triple fusion) is unique to angiosperms.
The endosperm of angiosperms is triploid (3n), formed by triple fusion.
Perisperm is the persistent remnant of the nucellus in seeds like black pepper and beet.
Scutellum is the single shield-shaped cotyledon of monocot seeds such as maize.
Coleoptile protects the emerging plumule and coleorhiza protects the radicle in cereals.
Vivipary (seed germinating inside the fruit) occurs in mangroves like Rhizophora.
Parthenocarpy produces seedless fruits (e.g. banana) without fertilisation.
Apomixis is seed formation without fertilisation, seen in some Asteraceae and grasses.
Polyembryony (multiple embryos in one seed) is common in Citrus.
The anther wall layers from outside are: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum.
Tapetum nourishes developing pollen grains and secretes Ubisch bodies.
Exine of pollen is made of sporopollenin, the most resistant organic substance known.
Pollen grains are stored as pollen banks at −196 °C in liquid nitrogen.
Wind-pollinated flowers produce enormous quantities of light, non-sticky pollen.
Insect-pollinated flowers are large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar.
The largest human cell is the ovum; the longest cell is the neuron.
Red blood cells lack nuclei and mitochondria in mammals, living about 120 days.
Platelets are cell fragments of megakaryocytes and live 8–10 days.
The SA node is the heart's natural pacemaker, generating about 72 impulses per minute.
Heart sounds: the first (lubb) is the closing of AV valves, the second (dupp) the closing of semilunar valves.
Cardiac output at rest is about 5 litres per minute (stroke volume × heart rate).
The normal blood pressure reading is 120/80 mm Hg.
Haemoglobin carries about 97% of oxygen; only 3% dissolves in plasma.
Each haemoglobin molecule binds four oxygen molecules cooperatively.
The partial pressure of oxygen in alveoli is about 104 mm Hg and in tissues about 40 mm Hg.
Carbon dioxide is carried mainly as bicarbonate ions (about 70%) in blood.
The enzyme carbonic anhydrase in RBCs speeds CO₂–bicarbonate conversion.
Chloride shift maintains electrical neutrality during CO₂ transport in RBCs.
Surfactant in alveoli reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse.
The diaphragm and external intercostal muscles drive quiet inspiration.
Juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin when blood pressure or sodium falls.
Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) opposes the RAAS by promoting sodium excretion.
ADH (vasopressin) increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct via aquaporins.
Oxytocin triggers milk ejection and uterine contraction during labour.
Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it — both from pancreatic islets.
Thyroxine (T4) requires iodine; its deficiency causes goitre and cretinism.
Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium by acting on bone, kidney and gut.
Calcitonin from thyroid C-cells lowers blood calcium, opposing PTH.
Myelin sheath is formed by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system.
The resting membrane potential of a neuron is about −70 mV, inside negative.

18 Sep 2026 — Takeda & Dr Reddy's Laboratories signed an exclusive deal to distribute Qdenga, India's first CDSCO-approved dengue vaccine — a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine against DENV-1 to DENV-4, two doses three months apart, for ages 4–60 — in the private market from the first half of 2027.

04 Sep 2026 — The NTA asked the AICTE to map IT infrastructure (functional computers, internet, power backup, CCTV, vacant space) at government institutions nationwide to build the exam-centre network for computer-based NEET-UG 2027.

14 Sep 2026 — NTA Director General Abhishek Singh said NEET will shift from pen-and-paper OMR to computer-based test (CBT) mode 'very soon', in line with the planned NEET-UG 2027 CBT rollout after the 2026 paper-leak controversy.

22 Sep 2026 — Columbia University researchers engineered a probiotic E. coli carrying cytosine deaminase to convert the harmless prodrug 5-FC into the chemotherapy drug 5-FU directly inside tumours, while also releasing an IL-15 superagonist and a PD-L1-blocking nanobody; tested against colorectal cancer and melanoma in mice (Science Translational Medicine).

25 Sep 2026 — Scientists reported the human neuronal noncoding RNA BC200 — a transposable 'jumping gene' — had escaped and integrated into the genome of the molluscum contagiosum poxvirus, the first clear wild case of a vertebrate transposon captured in a virus (Science).

26 Sep 2026 — A molecular 'self-destruct' switch was discovered: DNAJB12/DNAJB14 redox switching at the endoplasmic reticulum directs Bax/Bak-dependent apoptosis, a potential target against chemoresistance in cancer and ischemic injury of heart muscle (Redox Biology).

27 Sep 2026 — Researchers identified pTOS (para-tyramine-O-sulfate), an appetite-suppressing compound in python blood acting on the brain's regulatory centre, as a potential non-GLP-1 weight-loss therapy — a textbook case of comparative physiology inspiring medicine.

21 Sep 2026 — A Nature study showed the cohesin complex protects DNA replication forks from errors by reshaping fork contacts to aid fork slowing and reversal — a finding with implications for precision oncology since cohesin is mutated in several cancers.

08 Sep 2026 — NUS Medicine and St. Jude researchers used cryo-EM to resolve how the MFSD2B transporter exports the signalling lipid sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) from red blood cells and platelets into the bloodstream, where S1P keeps blood vessels healthy and guides immune-cell movement (Nature Communications).
